summary: Describes a mechanism to reduce redundant packet transmissions in the IS-IS routing protocol, as described in ISO 10589, for richly connected networks.

plainLanguage.summary: IS-IS routers learn about network changes by passing messages to each other. When every router is wired to every other router, the same message travels many more paths than it needs to. RFC 2973 describes how to mark links so that routers stop repeating the message along them.

questions: what is an is-is mesh group
subtitle: Marking fully connected links so that IS-IS stops repeating the same news along them

tldr.problem: IS-IS routers spread network updates by passing each link state PDU out every circuit except the one it arrived on. In a network where every router is wired to every other router, that sends N-2 extra copies of every update and buys almost no extra reliability.
tldr.mechanism: Each circuit gets a mesh attribute with the state meshInactive, meshBlocked or meshSet, and circuits marked meshSet with the same group number form a mesh group. The flooding rule is changed so an update received on a mesh circuit is not sent back out over the other circuits of the same mesh group.
tldr.outcome: The result is a flooding topology that is a subset of the physical topology. The mechanism depends on correct configuration, and the authors say they are not aware of any network running the numbered version.

facts.label: Extra transmissions per update
facts.value: N-2 in a full mesh of N systems

today: RFC 2973 is an Informational memo that has not been obsoleted or updated. It documents behaviour that already existed in deployed IS-IS implementations, so its value is as a description of how mesh groups work rather than as a new specification.

sections.title: The Flooding Problem in Full Meshes
sections.content:
In ATM or frame relay networks, routers are joined by virtual circuits, which are logical point-to-point links. Some organisations attach many routers so that every pair of them is connected. That arrangement is called a full mesh.

In IS-IS, a router that receives a new Link State PDU (LSP) stores it and floods it out every circuit except the one it arrived on. It does this by setting a send flag for each circuit it holds. In a full mesh of N routers, the standard mechanism produces N-2 extra transmissions of each LSP, a waste of bandwidth and processing effort with little gain in reliability.

The copies are unnecessary because every router in the mesh already has a direct link to the router that originated the update. The neighbour that forwards it is only delivering something the far end would have received anyway.
sections.plainLanguage: IS-IS routers spread news about network changes by passing it along every link they have. In a network where every router is connected to every other one, the same news gets passed around far more times than it needs to be. RFC 2973 describes how to stop the extra copies.

sections.title: Mesh Group States and Flooding Rules
sections.content:
A mesh group is a set of point-to-point circuits that give full connectivity to a set of routers. Each circuit gains two attributes: meshGroupEnabled, whose state is one of meshInactive, meshBlocked or meshSet, and an integer meshGroup that is valid only in the meshSet state. Circuits in the meshSet state that carry the same group number belong to the same mesh group.

LSPs are not flooded over circuits in the meshBlocked state, and an LSP received on a circuit is not flooded back out over the other circuits that belong to that circuit's mesh group. The memo rewrites the flooding rule in ISO 10589 clause 7.3.15.1 to say this, and changes the handling of Complete Sequence Number PDUs (CSNPs), the packets that keep neighbouring link state databases in step, in clause 7.3.15.3. LSPs that a router generates itself are not sent over meshBlocked circuits either.

Numbering the groups lets one large mesh be split into smaller full-mesh sub-topologies joined by transit circuits. Those transit circuits are left meshInactive, and the remaining circuits between groups are set to meshBlocked. The memo says this makes mesh groups more scalable.
sections.plainLanguage: Each link between routers gets a label. A link marked blocked carries no link state messages at all. A link marked mesh belongs to a group of routers that are all connected to each other, so a message arriving on one link of that group is not repeated along the others. Links that join one group to another stay normal and carry the message onward.

sections.title: Drawbacks and Practical Use
sections.content:
The memo is direct about the cost of the feature. It is a simple mechanism that relies on correct user configuration. If a combination of configuration and link failures results in a partitioned flooding topology, LSPs are not sent in a timely fashion, which may lead to routing loops or black holes.

Numbered mesh groups also add complexity and depend on static configuration, which makes topologies brittle. Losing a transit link can partition LSP flooding in unpredictable ways, and the periodic CSNPs needed to resynchronise databases become large and consume bandwidth in large networks.

The authors say they are not aware of any networks that have deployed numbered mesh groups. Instead, administrators set links to the meshBlocked state to prune the flooding topology, an arrangement the memo calls "poor man's mesh groups". It lists possible improvements, such as negotiating the mesh attributes when an adjacency starts and electing active transit links dynamically, and places them outside its own scope.
sections.plainLanguage: This shortcut only works if the network is configured correctly, and a mistake or a broken link can stop updates from reaching some routers. The authors say nobody seems to use the full numbered version; in practice people just block the extra links, which the memo calls 'poor man's mesh groups'.

sections.title: Interoperation with Other Routers
sections.content:
Mesh groups do not alter the content of any packet. A router that does not implement them sees no different packets and no new type-length-value fields. The only impact is that additional CSNPs arrive on some point-to-point links, and a conformant implementation is expected to respond correctly to extra CSNPs.

The memo notes that the behaviours it describes are backwards compatible with implementations that do not support the feature, because the change is in what a router sends, not in what the packets contain.
sections.plainLanguage: Other routers do not need any new software. They receive a few extra packets and answer them as usual, which is what makes the feature safe to use next to routers that know nothing about it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo states that it raises no new security issues for IS-IS, and it adds nothing further to that statement. Mesh groups are set by configuration on each circuit rather than by an exchange between routers, and they add no packets and no fields to what travels on the network.

The risk the memo does describe is misconfiguration, and it treats that as an operational drawback rather than a security problem.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo says it does not raise any new security problems for IS-IS. It changes no packet content and adds no new fields, so what travels between routers stays the same as before.

items.label: Normal circuit
items.desc: The standard flooding rule applies: the update goes out on every circuit except the one it arrived on.

items.label: In a mesh group
items.desc: The circuit carries a mesh group number, and an update arriving on it is not sent back out over the other circuits of that group.

items.label: Pruned circuit
items.desc: Link state PDUs are not flooded over the circuit, and generated LSPs are not sent on it.
